aboutAuthor: Al Ries and Jack Trout are the positioning pioneers whose thinking shaped modern marketing strategy. Their 22 'laws' distill decades of consulting into short, ruthless principles about how minds and markets work.

points.heading: It's better to be first than to be better
points.body: The Law of Leadership: being first in a category beats having a superior product. Charles Lindbergh was first across the Atlantic; who was second? Categories are remembered by their pioneers, so create a new category if you can't be first in the old one.

points.heading: Marketing is a battle of perceptions
points.body: The best product doesn't win — the first perception does. Marketing isn't about facts argued persuasively; it's about what already exists in the prospect's mind. Once a mind is made up, changing it is nearly impossible.

points.heading: Own a word in the prospect's mind
points.body: The Law of Focus: the most powerful concept in marketing is owning one word — Mercedes owns 'engineering,' Volvo owns 'safety,' FedEx overnight. Burn that word into memory and defend it forever.

points.heading: The Law of the Opposite
points.body: If you're number two, your strategy is determined by the leader: turn their strength into weakness. Avis's 'We're number two, so we try harder' converted inferiority into honesty. Don't attack strength where it's strong — reframe it.

points.heading: Never extend the line
points.body: Line extension puts your name on everything and thereby on nothing. More is less: every product you add dilutes the meaning of the brand. When you want to enter a new category, launch a new brand instead.

points.heading: Failure is expected — admit it fast
points.body: Companies punish failure and thereby breed cover-ups that compound losses. The Law of Failure says to accept mistakes early and cheaply. Candor is disarming: admitting a shortcoming builds trust that perfection never earns.

insights: Ries & Trout earlier wrote 'Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind,' the seed of this book.
The book's examples (IBM, Miller, Burger King) read as case studies of laws obeyed and broken.
Critics call the laws 'immutable'; the authors respond that breaking them proves the point.
conclusion: The 22 Immutable Laws of Marketing argues that markets live in minds, not spreadsheets: be first or create a category, own one word, exploit the leader's opposite, and resist line extension. Simple rules, brutally hard to follow.
